answer: Motorcycle gloves fit when your fingertips just touch the ends with your fingers curled around a grip, the knuckle armor sits squarely over your knuckles in the riding position, the palm has no loose folds, and the wrist closure is snug enough that the glove can't be pulled off in a slide.
intro: Motorcycle gloves are protective gear, so they have to stay on your hands in a crash and keep armor where it belongs. They also have to let you work the clutch and brake levers precisely. Judge them with your hands in the riding position, fingers curled as if holding the grips, not with your hands flat.

checklist.good: With your fingers curled around an imaginary grip, your fingertips just touch the ends of the glove without pressing.
checklist.tooTight: Too short: your fingertips jam into the ends when you curl your fingers, which leads to numbness on longer rides.
checklist.tooLoose: Too long: there's spare material at the tips that catches on levers and switches.

checklist.good: When you grip, the hard knuckle protector sits centered over your knuckles and doesn't press into them.
checklist.tooTight: The armor presses hard into the knuckles or the back of the hand when you make a fist.
checklist.tooLoose: The armor slides off to the side or sits behind your knuckles on the back of the hand.

checklist.good: The palm and any slider pad lie smooth against your hand, with no folds when you grip the bar.
checklist.tooTight: The palm stretches tight and pulls the fingers back, making it tiring to hold the grip.
checklist.tooLoose: Loose material bunches in your palm when you grip, which hurts feel and causes hot spots.

checklist.good: You can reach and pull the clutch and brake levers with two or four fingers without the glove resisting.
checklist.tooTight: The fingers feel stiff or the seams bite between your fingers when you pull a lever.
checklist.tooLoose: Fingers twist inside the glove, so you can't feel the levers precisely.

checklist.good: The thumb reaches the end of its stall and you can easily reach the turn signal and horn buttons.
checklist.tooTight: The thumb is pulled toward the palm or the seam at its base digs in.
checklist.tooLoose: The thumb tip is empty, making switchgear clumsy.

checklist.good: With the wrist strap fastened, you can't pull the glove off by tugging on its fingertips.
checklist.tooTight: The strap restricts your wrist movement or blood flow.
checklist.tooLoose: The glove can be tugged off with the wrist strap fastened, so it could come off in a slide.

variations.heading: Gauntlet, short-cuff and seasonal gloves
variations.intro: Glove style decides how the cuff works with your jacket. The finger and palm fit stays the same.

items.name: Gauntlet (long-cuff) gloves
items.text: Cover the wrist and lower forearm and are worn over the jacket sleeve, which keeps wind and rain from blowing up the arm. Check that the gauntlet closes over your sleeve without being forced.

items.name: Short-cuff gloves
items.text: End at the wrist and are worn under the jacket sleeve. The jacket cuff should cover the glove cuff without a gap of bare skin when you reach for the bars.

items.name: Racing gloves
items.text: Usually have pre-curved fingers, extra armor and a double wrist closure. They're cut for the riding position, so they may feel awkward with your hand flat.

items.name: Winter and waterproof gloves
items.text: Insulation and membranes add bulk. Allow a little more room at the fingertips, but check that you can still operate the levers precisely.

items.name: Summer and mesh gloves
items.text: Thin and well ventilated. Fit should be close, because thin leather and mesh stretch with use.

measure.heading: How to measure for motorcycle gloves
measure.intro: Most brands size by palm circumference and sometimes hand length.
steps: Use a soft tape measure on your throttle hand (usually the right), which is often slightly larger.
Measure around your palm just below the knuckles, leaving out the thumb.
Measure your hand length from the tip of your middle finger to the crease at the base of the palm.
Check both measurements against the brand's size chart.
If circumference and length point to different sizes, choose by length for fingertip fit and by circumference for palm fit, then try both on.
measure.tip: Try gloves on while sitting on your bike, or with your hands curled as if gripping, and work the levers if the shop allows.

problems.fix: The gloves are too short when your fingers curl. Size up or try a pre-curved design.

problems.problem: Knuckle armor presses into your hand
problems.fix: The armor isn't lined up with your knuckles. Try a size where it sits centered when you grip, or a model with softer, segmented armor.

problems.problem: The gauntlet won't close over your jacket sleeve
problems.fix: Look for gloves with wider gauntlets or wear a short-cuff glove under the sleeve instead.

problems.problem: Gloves are hard to get on with sweaty hands
problems.fix: Thin glove liners help, and gloves with a wrist-to-cuff vent make it easier. Don't size up just for this.

extra.heading: Break-in and stretch
extra.body: Leather motorcycle gloves usually ease slightly as they break in, especially across the palm. Textile gloves stretch less. New leather gloves should start snug but not painful, and you should still be able to operate the levers from the first ride.

extra.heading: When to replace motorcycle gloves
extra.body: Replace gloves after a crash in which they slid on pavement, or when the palm is worn thin, seams are opening, or the wrist strap no longer holds. Armor that's cracked or loose should also be replaced.

picks.label: Leather gauntlet motorcycle gloves
picks.why: Maximum coverage and a seal over the jacket sleeve for touring and sport riding.

picks.label: Short-cuff motorcycle gloves with knuckle armor
picks.why: Easier on and off for commuting, with protection over the knuckles.
picks.query: short cuff motorcycle gloves knuckle protection

picks.label: Waterproof winter motorcycle gloves
picks.why: Insulated and sealed for cold-weather riding; allow a little extra fingertip room.

picks.label: Mesh summer motorcycle gloves
picks.why: Ventilated for hot weather while keeping palm and knuckle protection.

faqs.a: Snug, not tight. They should stay on with the wrist strap closed and the armor should sit over your knuckles, but you should be able to grip and pull levers comfortably.

faqs.q: How much room should be at the fingertips of motorcycle gloves?
faqs.a: With your fingers curled as if gripping, your fingertips should just touch the ends. If they press, the gloves are too short.
Leather gloves stretch a little, mostly in the palm. Textile and mesh gloves stretch less. Buy them snug, but not painful.

faqs.q: Should motorcycle gloves go over or under the jacket?
faqs.a: Gauntlet gloves go over the jacket sleeve; short-cuff gloves go under it. Either way, there should be no exposed skin when you reach for the bars.

faqs.q: How do I know if motorcycle gloves are too big?
faqs.a: If you can pull them off with the wrist strap closed, if the armor slides off your knuckles, or if the palm bunches when you grip, they're too big.
